newsitem.title: EASTERN EUROPE: Emerging Europe Advertising & Media Digest-Aug 5.
newsitem.headline: Emerging Europe Advertising & Media Digest-Aug 5.

text.p: REUTERS EMERGING EUROPE PRESS DIGEST FOR ADVERTISING & MEDIA
Weekly Press Digest from Central and Eastern Europe on Advertising, Marketing, the Media, the Internet, Brand-name Products and Consumer Trends.
ADVERTISING & MARKETING:

-- Procter & Gamble in the Czech Republic says it is replacing the Azuritek bunny on television commercials for its Azurit washing powder with a fuzzy blue dot. The blue dot, named Kulicka -- meaning little dot -- will be the same light blue colour as the bunny and have the same charm, Procter & Gamble says. (Strategie News, July 30 - August 6, 1997)

-- Magyar RTL, which won a licence for one of Hungary's new television stations, has tapped the Ammirati Puris Lintas advertising agency to prepare its introductory advertising campaign, Lintas says. (Vilaggazdasag, July 30, 1997)

-- Newspapers claimed a 30.9 percent share in Poland's advertising market in 1996, according to a a report by Amer Nielsen Research. A study by the Gazeta Wyborcza showed newspapers with a 44.5 percent share of the Polish advertising market. Dziennik Prawa i Gospodarki, July 31, 1997)

-- Television advertising revenue in the Czech Republic rose 17.8 percent in the 1997 first half from the year-ago period, A-Connect reports. Radio advertising turnover increased 8.2 percent in the first-half over the 1996 period, and print media advertising increased nearly 17.9 percent, A-Connect says.
(Strategie News, July 30 - August 6, 1997)

-- Hungarian radio station MR Rt signs an agreement with the Hungarian Olympic Committee to become the official radio station of the Hungarian Olympic team. Under the deal, MR Rt will air advertising slots for the Olympic Committee worth 10 million forints ($50,000) each year. (Vilaggazdasag, July 30, 1997)

-- Following a survey which showed Russian 10- 15-year-olds spend 40.3 percent of their money buying sweets, the State Anti-monopoly Committee warns that advertising regulations are not tight enough to prevent companies from using cartoon characters and toys to attract young customers. The advertising industry's Public Council sets up a committee to implement western-style self-regulation. (Kapital - July 30 - August 5)
MEDIA & THE INTERNET:

-- MTM-SBS Televizio RT and Magyar RTL, the winners for the licences for Hungary's two new television channels, have paid in 30 percent of their 10-year concession fees into the broadcasting fund. The money, totaling more than 5 billion forints, will be allocated to Hungarian Television, Duna TV and the National Radio and Television Board (ORTT). (Vilaggazdasag, July 31, 1997)

-- The Bulgarian Constitutional Court agrees to review an appeal by the main opposition Socialist Party, which says parliament's replacement of heads of the state media in mid-July was contrary to the countrys radio and television law. (24 Chasa, August 1, 1997)

-- The private Media Trans agency, which acts as mediator between Bulgarian National Television (BNT) and advertising agencies, owes the television station some $240,000, BNTs new marketing director Petar Korumbashev says. (Capital, July 28-August 3,1997)

-- Bulgarian state radio has the highest rating among the countrys radio stations with 19.1 percent of the radio audience, says a survey. It is followed by the private FM+ music radio station with 15.3 percent and the private Express radio with 12.7 percent, the survey says. (Pari, July 30, 1997)
BRAND-NAME PRODUCTS & MARKETS:

-- The Czech Republic's Starobrno Brewery introduces, Cerveny Drak, the world's first red beer. Cerveny Drak, or Red Dragon, is currently being sold only in select pubs, clubs and discos. The beer features a stopper that looks like a fuse or a grenade. (Reflex, July 30, 1997)

-- Danone yoghurt and Laciate milk are consumer favourites in Poland, with about 47 percent of Poles buying Danone yoghurts and 17 percent buying Laciate, a survey by the PBS polling institute says. (Rzeczpospolita, July 28, 1997)

-- Finnish vodka Koskenkorva is gaining popularity in the Czech Republic with its six flavours of 21 percent vodka. Koskenkorva Peach is the favourite, followed by Koskenkorva Lemon. Cranberry-flavoured Koskenkorva Vartgass is also well liked. (Pravo, July 29, 1997)

-- Poland's pharmaceutical market remains underdeveloped compared with other countries in the region and is open for more investment, ING Barings says in a report. The average Pole consumes $40 worth of pharmaceutics each year, ING Barings reports. (Rzeczpospolita, July 29, 1997)

-- Coca-Cola remains the preferred non-alcoholic beverage in the Czech Republic, with 16 percent of respondents to a new survey by Aisa listing it as their favourite. Other favourites listed were Mattoni, preferred by 14 percent, Good Water at six percent, Fanta at six percent, Hanacka Kyselka at four percent, and Pepsi at four percent. Younger people preferred Coca-Cola and Fanta, while older people preferred Mattoni and Good Water, according to the survey of 1,142 15- to 69-year olds.(Pravo, July 29, 1997)
CONSUMER TRENDS:

-- Czech-Austrian Ronja s.r.o. opens the largest duty free shop in Europe at the border crossing Hate u Znojma. The shop is part of Excalibur City, a 300,000-square-metre area containing two duty free shops, a shopping centre, restaurants, a petrol station and a race track, Smart Communications reports. (Hospodarske Noviny, July 30, 1997)

-- Hungary's retail trade and catering sectors posted 8.4 percent year-on-year growth in nominal terms in the first four months of 1997, with consolidated turnover rising to 864.4 billion forints. But based on inflation-adjusted prices, turnover fell 7.7 percent the Industry and Trade Ministry reports. The ministry says the volume of retail trade turnover may increase by one or two percent in the remaining part of this year. (Napi Gazdasag, July 28, 1997)
